# Worksheet: people who know something

**~50 minutes**

In every model this week, people have behaved the same way from the first day of
the epidemic to the last. Real populations do not. When infection turns up nearby,
people change what they do, and they change it on the basis of whatever they
happen to know.

This session takes the grid model from the previous session and gives each person
one rule of that kind: *if I can see infection around me, I take precautions*.
Then it asks a question that only an individual-level model can answer. The same
precautions, taken by the same number of people, protect a population by
different amounts depending on **what those people can see**.

The model, the parameters and the grid are the ones you built in the previous
session. What is new is a rule about behaviour and a way of counting how much
precaution the population takes.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-setup
using Agents

using StableRNGs
using Statistics

    bytes::Vector{UInt8}

end
Base.show(io::IO, ::MIME"text/html", a::Animation) =
    print(io, "<video controls autoplay loop ",

println("Julia ", VERSION)

    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

const N = 1000
const β = 0.05
const c = 10.0
const γ = 0.25

@agent struct Person(GridAgent{2})
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end

susceptible_count(model) = count(p.status == :S for p in allagents(model))
infected_count(model) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(model))
recovered_count(model) = count(p.status == :R for p in allagents(model))
```

`StableRNG` fixes the random *stream*, and that is less than full
reproducibility. It does not fix what the code draws from that stream:
`shuffle`, `Poisson` sampling and `rand(rng, collection)` are implementations in
Julia's standard library and in `Distributions.jl`, and any of them may consume a
different number of values, or combine them differently, in another version. So
exact digits need the Julia version and the resolved package set, not the seed
alone. Both are recorded: the setup cell prints the Julia version and the package
versions, and the exact resolution is committed in this repository's
`Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml`. On any other combination expect the
conclusions to hold and the digits not to.

## Part A — agents who react (~15 min)

The behaviour rule is one sentence: **a susceptible person who can see at least
`m` infectious people within `info_radius` cells takes precautions for that step,
and the chance of catching the infection from any one contact falls from
$\beta$ to $\beta(1-\alpha)$.**

Three numbers describe it, and each one is a modelling assumption:

- `info_radius`, how far the person's information reaches;
- `m`, how many cases it takes before they change their behaviour;
- `α`, how much good the precautions do. $\alpha = 0.5$ halves the chance of
  transmission per contact.

The same rule is written three ways here, because Part C needs to compare them.
`:none` is the model from the previous session. `:local` is the rule above.
`:national` reacts instead to the prevalence $I/N$ in the whole population, the
way a person watching the news would. Note what the model grants that rule: the
true prevalence, seen at once and without under-reporting or delay. A real
national figure is none of those things, which is the subject of the observation
models session.

Name all three branches explicitly and reject anything else. A rule the function
does not recognise is a mistake, most likely a typo in a keyword argument, and it
should stop the run rather than quietly select one of the three for you.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-a1
function is_aware(person, model)
    if model.information == :none
        return false
    elseif model.information == :national
        return model.prevalence >= model.θ
    elseif model.information == :local
        # TODO: aware when at least m of the people within info_radius are infectious
        return false
    else
        throw(ArgumentError(
            "unknown information rule $(model.information); " *
            "expected :none, :local or :national"))
    end
end
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A, the awareness rule

```julia
return count(a -> a.status == :I,
             nearby_agents(person, model, model.info_radius)) >= model.m
```

`nearby_agents` is the same function you used to find contacts in the previous
session, with a different radius: the people you *hear about* need not be the
people you *meet*.
:::

The rules themselves change in one place only, where $\beta$ is used.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-a2
function agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        transmission = is_aware(person, model) ? model.β * (1 - model.α) : model.β
        neighbours = collect(nearby_agents(person, model, model.radius))
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = rand(abmrng(model), neighbours)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < transmission
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I
        if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
            person.next_status = :R
        end
    end
    return nothing
end

function model_step!(model)
    model.aware_days += model.Δt *
        count(p -> p.status == :S && is_aware(p, model), allagents(model))
    for person in allagents(model)
        person.status = person.next_status
    end
    model.prevalence = infected_count(model) / N
    return nothing
end
```

`model_step!` now does two things besides committing the statuses. It adds up
**aware person-days**, the number of susceptible people taking precautions times
the length of the step, and it records the current prevalence, which the
`:national` rule reads on the next step.

The order of those three operations matters. `agent_step!` decided this step's
transmission using the statuses and the prevalence as they stood at the *start*
of the step, so the count of aware people has to be taken before either is
updated. Count after the commit and you would be reporting the precautions of a
population that has already moved on. That running total is how much precaution
the population took, and Part C uses it to compare the rules on equal terms.

Model-wide values that change during a run have to live in a dictionary rather
than the named tuple of the previous session, because a named tuple cannot be
written to.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-a3
function initialize_model(seed; information = :none, α = 0.5, m = 1,
                          info_radius = 3, θ = 0.05,
                          I0 = 10, radius = 2, Δt = 0.1)
    space = GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic = true, metric = :chebyshev)
    model = StandardABM(
        Person, space;
        agent_step!, model_step!,
        properties = Dict(
            :β => β, :c => c, :γ => γ, :Δt => Δt, :radius => radius,
            :information => information, :α => α, :m => m,
            :info_radius => info_radius, :θ => θ,
            :prevalence => I0 / N, :aware_days => 0.0,
        ),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for position in positions(model)
        add_agent!(position, model; status = :S, next_status = :S)
    end
    for id in shuffle(abmrng(model), collect(allids(model)))[1:I0]
        model[id].status = :I
        model[id].next_status = :I
    end
    return model
end

function run_epidemic(seed; max_steps = 10_000, kwargs...)
    model = initialize_model(seed; kwargs...)
    infectious = Int[infected_count(model)]
    while infectious[end] > 0
        length(infectious) > max_steps && error(
            "still infectious after $max_steps steps ($(max_steps * model.Δt) time " *
            "units); raise max_steps. A response too weak to interrupt transmission " *
            "can run far longer than the settings used here.")
        step!(model, 1)
        push!(infectious, infected_count(model))
    end
    return (; peak = maximum(infectious),
              final = recovered_count(model),
              aware_days = model.aware_days,
              duration = (length(infectious) - 1) * model.Δt,
              infectious)
end

replicate_seeds = 7000 .+ (1:8)

function summarise(; kwargs...)
    runs = [run_epidemic(seed; kwargs...) for seed in replicate_seeds]
    return (; peak = round(mean(r.peak for r in runs); digits = 1),
              final = round(mean(r.final for r in runs); digits = 1),
              final_sd = round(std([r.final for r in runs]); digits = 1),
              aware_days = round(Int, mean(r.aware_days for r in runs)),
              finals = [Float64(r.final) for r in runs],
              aware_each = [r.aware_days for r in runs])
end
```

`summarise` keeps the eight per-seed values as well as their means. Part B needs
them, because a mean on its own says nothing about how well eight runs pin it
down.

`run_epidemic` runs until nobody is infectious, so every number it reports is a
*final* one. The step cap is a safety net rather than a horizon: if it is ever
reached the function raises an error instead of returning a half-finished
epidemic, which matters because a weak response can stretch an epidemic well past
the durations seen at the default settings. A run that fails to finish should be
reported, not silently cut short.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-a4
baseline = summarise(information = :none)
local_rule = summarise(information = :local, m = 1, α = 0.5)

check("awareness lowers the peak", local_rule.peak < 0.6 * baseline.peak)
check("awareness lowers the final size", local_rule.final < 0.5 * baseline.final)
check("the baseline population never takes precautions",
      baseline.aware_days == 0.0)

(; baseline, local_rule)
```

Look at the population rather than the totals. Aware people are drawn in orange.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06b-snapshot
#| fig-cap: "One run with the local rule, at three times. Blue is susceptible, orange is a susceptible person taking precautions, red infectious, green recovered. Precautions are concentrated around the infected patches rather than spread across the grid, which is what Part C then measures."
snapshot_model = initialize_model(7001; information = :local, m = 1, α = 0.5)
awareness_colour(p) =
    p.status === :I ? :firebrick :
    p.status === :R ? :seagreen :
    is_aware(p, snapshot_model) ? :orange : :steelblue

fig = Figure(size = (1000, 250))
previous = 0.0
for (j, t) in enumerate((3.0, 8.0, 20.0))
    step!(snapshot_model, round(Int, (t - previous) / 0.1))
    previous = t
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; title = "t = $t", aspect = DataAspect())
    abmplot!(ax, snapshot_model; agent_color = awareness_colour,
             agent_marker = :rect, agent_size = 7)
    hidedecorations!(ax)
end
fig
```

### Does the extra information ring do anything?

The default `info_radius` is 3 while contacts come from radius 2, so a person
hears about a ring of people they can never meet. It is natural to read that as
advance warning. Before believing it, measure it: run the same rule at
`info_radius = 3` and at `info_radius = 2`, changing nothing else.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-a5
# Run the two radii in lockstep and compare every agent's status at every step.
# Equal S, I and R totals would not be enough: two runs could put the same
# numbers of people in each compartment and disagree about which people.
function compare_radii(seed; m, α = 0.5, radii = (3, 2), max_steps = 10_000)
    models = [initialize_model(seed; information = :local, m = m, α = α, info_radius = r)
              for r in radii]
    statuses(model) = [model[id].status for id in 1:nagents(model)]
    agree = statuses(models[1]) == statuses(models[2])
    steps = 0
    while any(infected_count(model) > 0 for model in models)
        steps += 1
        steps > max_steps && error("still infectious after $max_steps steps; raise max_steps")
        foreach(model -> step!(model, 1), models)
        agree &= statuses(models[1]) == statuses(models[2])
    end
    return (; agree,
              final = map(recovered_count, models),
              aware_days = map(model -> model.aware_days, models))
end

comparisons = Dict(m => [compare_radii(seed; m = m) for seed in replicate_seeds]
                   for m in (1, 2))

check("at m = 1 every agent holds the same status at every step under both radii",
      all(c.agree for c in comparisons[1]))
check("the two radii still record different amounts of precaution",
      all(c.aware_days[1] > c.aware_days[2] for c in comparisons[1]))
check("at m = 2 the two populations diverge, in every seed",
      all(!c.agree for c in comparisons[2]))

[(; m,
    final_info_radius_3 = round(mean(c.final[1] for c in cs); digits = 1),
    final_info_radius_2 = round(mean(c.final[2] for c in cs); digits = 1),
    aware_days_3 = round(Int, mean(c.aware_days[1] for c in cs)),
    aware_days_2 = round(Int, mean(c.aware_days[2] for c in cs)))
 for (m, cs) in ((1, comparisons[1]), (2, comparisons[2]))]
```

The `m = 2` check says only that the two populations *differ*. It says nothing
about which is better, so ask that separately, and ask it as a paired contrast:
the two radii share a seed, so subtract seed by seed rather than comparing two
column means.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-a6
function paired_final_contrast(cs; reps = 4000, seed = 11)
    differences = [Float64(c.final[1] - c.final[2]) for c in cs]
    rng = StableRNG(seed)
    n = length(differences)
    resampled = map(1:reps) do _
        mean(differences[rand(rng, 1:n, n)])
    end
    return (; per_seed_difference = Int.(differences),
              mean_difference = round(mean(differences); digits = 1),
              seeds_favouring_radius_3 = count(<(0), differences),
              interval = (round(quantile(resampled, 0.025); digits = 1),
                          round(quantile(resampled, 0.975); digits = 1)))
end

paired_final_contrast(comparisons[2])
```

At `m = 1` the two runs are not merely similar. Every one of the thousand people
holds the same status at every step under both radii. The aware person-days do not
match, and at `m = 2` the populations come apart.

## Part B — how soon, and how hard (~15 min)

Two of the three numbers are about the behaviour rather than the disease. `m`
says how much evidence someone needs before acting, and `α` says how much good
acting does. Sweep them one at a time.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-b1
trigger_sweep = [(; m, summarise(information = :local, m = m, α = 0.5)...)
                 for m in (1, 2, 3)]
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-b2
strength_sweep = [(; α, summarise(information = :local, m = 1, α = α)...)
                  for α in (0.25, 0.5, 0.75)]
```

A mechanism that halves the epidemic is worth more if fewer people had to change
their behaviour to get there. Define that ratio: infections averted for each
person-day of precautions, measured against the population that does nothing.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-b3
# TODO: infections averted per aware person-day, against the no-awareness baseline
#       Use the per-seed vectors `finals` and `aware_each`, not `final` and
#       `aware_days`: those two are rounded for display.
averted_per_aware_day(result) = 0.0

check("a rule that changes nothing averts nothing",
      averted_per_aware_day((; finals = baseline.finals,
                               aware_each = ones(length(baseline.finals)))) == 0.0)
check("of the three triggers, acting on the first case has the highest point estimate",
      averted_per_aware_day(trigger_sweep[1]) >
      maximum(averted_per_aware_day(r) for r in trigger_sweep[2:end]))

[(; description = "m = $(r.m)", averted = round(averted_per_aware_day(r); digits = 3))
 for r in trigger_sweep]
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-b4
[(; description = "α = $(r.α)", averted = round(averted_per_aware_day(r); digits = 3))
 for r in strength_sweep]
```

Those are eight-run point estimates and nothing more. Both the numerator and the
denominator are averages over the same eight noisy runs, and the uncertainty of a
ratio of estimated averages is not captured by the uncertainty of either component
alone, so the whole ratio has to be recomputed in every bootstrap sample. Reading
an order off three such numbers is not a comparison. Quantify each estimate's
uncertainty first, then compare the settings using the paired contrast intervals
below.

Every setting uses the same `replicate_seeds`, so the runs pair up across
settings and across the baseline. Resample the eight seeds with replacement,
recompute the whole ratio from whichever seeds were drawn, and read the interval
off the spread of those recomputations. Resampling seeds, rather than resampling
each setting on its own, is what keeps that pairing intact. Note what the pairing
does and does not achieve: it makes the interval account for whatever dependence there
is, which is the correct procedure, but it does not automatically make the
interval narrower. Resampling independently can come out either too wide or too
narrow, depending on the sign of the covariance between the paired outcomes.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-b5
function averted_interval(result; reps = 4000, seed = 11)
    rng = StableRNG(seed)
    n = length(result.finals)
    samples = map(1:reps) do _
        drawn = rand(rng, 1:n, n)
        taken = mean(result.aware_each[drawn])
        taken == 0 ? NaN :
            (mean(baseline.finals[drawn]) - mean(result.finals[drawn])) / taken
    end
    usable = filter(isfinite, samples)
    isempty(usable) && return nothing   # a rule nobody ever acts on has no ratio
    return (round(quantile(usable, 0.025); digits = 3),
            round(quantile(usable, 0.975); digits = 3))
end

[(; description = "m = $(r.m)",
    averted = round(averted_per_aware_day(r); digits = 3),
    interval = averted_interval(r)) for r in trigger_sweep]
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-b6
[(; description = "α = $(r.α)",
    averted = round(averted_per_aware_day(r); digits = 3),
    interval = averted_interval(r)) for r in strength_sweep]
```

An interval around a single setting answers "does this rule avert anything at
all?", by asking whether it excludes zero. It does **not** answer "do two
settings differ?". Two overlapping intervals are perfectly compatible with a
difference that is itself well away from zero, because the difference has its own
sampling distribution and the two settings share their seeds. So bootstrap the
*contrast* directly: resample the seeds once, recompute both settings' ratios from
the same drawn seeds, and take the difference.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-b7
function contrast_interval(first_rule, second_rule; reps = 4000, seed = 11)
    rng = StableRNG(seed)
    n = length(first_rule.finals)
    value(drawn, rule) = (mean(baseline.finals[drawn]) - mean(rule.finals[drawn])) /
                         mean(rule.aware_each[drawn])
    samples = map(1:reps) do _
        drawn = rand(rng, 1:n, n)
        value(drawn, first_rule) - value(drawn, second_rule)
    end
    usable = filter(isfinite, samples)
    isempty(usable) && return nothing
    return (round(quantile(usable, 0.025); digits = 3),
            round(quantile(usable, 0.975); digits = 3))
end

[(; contrast = "m = $(a.m) minus m = $(b.m)",
    difference = round(averted_per_aware_day(a) - averted_per_aware_day(b); digits = 3),
    interval = contrast_interval(a, b))
 for (a, b) in ((trigger_sweep[1], trigger_sweep[2]),
                (trigger_sweep[1], trigger_sweep[3]),
                (trigger_sweep[2], trigger_sweep[3]))]
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-b8
[(; contrast = "α = $(a.α) minus α = $(b.α)",
    difference = round(averted_per_aware_day(a) - averted_per_aware_day(b); digits = 3),
    interval = contrast_interval(a, b))
 for (a, b) in ((strength_sweep[3], strength_sweep[2]),
                (strength_sweep[2], strength_sweep[1]),
                (strength_sweep[3], strength_sweep[1]))]
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

```julia
averted_per_aware_day(result) =

```

`baseline.finals` holds the eight per-seed numbers infected when nobody reacts, so
the numerator is how many infections this rule prevented. Take the means here
rather than reusing `result.final` and `result.aware_days`, which `summarise`
already rounded for display: round at the end, not in the middle.

## Part C — the same behaviour, different information (~20 min)

Here is the comparison the session has been building towards.

The `:national` rule is the same behaviour as the `:local` one. The same
precautions, the same $\alpha$, the same on-or-off decision. The only difference
is what a person is looking at: the prevalence $I/N$ in the whole population,
which this model hands them perfectly and without delay, rather than the people
around them.

Comparing them needs a fair basis, because either rule can be made stronger by
having more people take precautions for longer. Aware person-days is that basis:
it measures how much precaution was taken, not what that precaution cost.
Choose the national threshold $\theta$ so that the national rule has the
population take about the same amount of precaution as the local rule does. Try a
few values.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-c1
# TODO: choose θ so the national rule produces about the same aware person-days
#       as the local rule. Try 0.10, then 0.05, then 0.02.
θ_matched = 0.10

national_rule = summarise(information = :national, θ = θ_matched, α = 0.5)

precaution_ratio = national_rule.aware_days / local_rule.aware_days
check("the two rules now take about the same amount of precaution",
      0.75 < precaution_ratio < 1.35)

(; local_rule, national_rule, precaution_ratio = round(precaution_ratio; digits = 2))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C, matching the precaution taken

A threshold of 0.05 means people react once 5% of the population is infectious.
Lowering it makes them react sooner and stay careful for longer, so the aware
person-days go up as $\theta$ goes down.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-c2
matched = [(; rule = "local, m = 1", local_rule.final, local_rule.aware_days),
           (; rule = "national, θ = $θ_matched",
              national_rule.final, national_rule.aware_days)]

check("the local rule ends with a far smaller epidemic",
      local_rule.final < 0.4 * national_rule.final)

matched
```

Part B built a tool for exactly this comparison, so use it rather than reading two
separate intervals against each other: contrast the two rules directly, on the same
resampled seeds.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-c2b
(; contrast = "local m = 1 minus national θ = $θ_matched",
   difference = round(averted_per_aware_day(local_rule) -
                      averted_per_aware_day(national_rule); digits = 3),
   interval = contrast_interval(local_rule, national_rule))
```

### Optional — watch the two rules side by side

The tables say the two rules take a similar amount of precaution and end in very
different places. This cell shows both runs at once, same seed, same colours as
before, with each panel's title carrying the running counts. It uses your
`θ_matched`, so change that and the right-hand panel changes with it.

Watch two things: **where** the orange is, and **when** it is there at all.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06b-video-comparison
#| error: true
comparison = (
    (initialize_model(7001; information = :local, m = 1, α = 0.5), "local, m = 1"),
    (initialize_model(7001; information = :national, θ = θ_matched, α = 0.5),
     "national, θ = $θ_matched"),
)

# Nobody moves, so one person stays in each cell for the whole run and the grid
# can be drawn as a matrix of codes rather than a thousand markers.
function status_codes(model)
    codes = Matrix{Int}(undef, 40, 25)
    for position in positions(model)
        person = model[id_in_position(position, model)]
        codes[position...] = person.status === :I ? 3 :
                             person.status === :R ? 4 :
                             is_aware(person, model) ? 2 : 1
    end
    return codes
end

comparison_frames = 150
steps_per_frame = 3

fig = Figure(size = (1100, 380))
grids = Observable[]
headings = Observable[]
for (j, (model, name)) in enumerate(comparison)
    push!(grids, Observable(status_codes(model)))
    push!(headings, Observable(name))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; aspect = DataAspect(), title = headings[j])
    heatmap!(ax, grids[j];
        colormap = cgrad([:steelblue, :orange, :firebrick, :seagreen];
                         categorical = true),
        colorrange = (0.5, 4.5))
    hidedecorations!(ax)
end

comparison_path = "abm-awareness-comparison.mp4"
record(fig, comparison_path, 1:comparison_frames; framerate = 15) do frame
    t = round((frame - 1) * steps_per_frame * 0.1; digits = 1)
    for (j, (model, name)) in enumerate(comparison)
        grids[j][] = status_codes(model)
        aware = count(p -> p.status == :S && is_aware(p, model), allagents(model))
        headings[j][] = "$name — t = $t, infectious $(infected_count(model)), " *
                        "taking care $aware"
        step!(model, steps_per_frame)
    end
end

Animation(read(comparison_path), 1100)
```

The clip runs to $t = 44.7$, long enough for the local epidemic to finish and for
the national threshold to have come and gone.

While `θ_matched` is still the starting 0.10, the right-hand panel never turns
orange: the epidemic here peaks near 70 infectious people in a thousand, so a
threshold of 10% is never crossed and the rule does nothing at all. That is worth
seeing once before you lower it.

If both panels look identical, that is correct rather than a bug. A local rule
whose `is_aware` still returns `false` and a national rule whose threshold is
never reached are the same model, and on the same seed they produce the same
epidemic frame for frame. The panels separate once Part A's `is_aware` is
finished and `θ_matched` is low enough to fire.

Neither rule has to be used at one setting. Sweeping both gives a curve of what
each rule achieves for the precaution it asks of people.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06b-cost
#| fig-cap: "Final epidemic size against the precaution taken to achieve it, for the local rule at three trigger levels and the national rule at four thresholds. Both rules use the same precautions. Across these tested settings, the local-rule points achieve smaller final sizes at similar or lower aware person-days."
national_sweep = [(; θ, summarise(information = :national, θ = θ, α = 0.5)...)
                  for θ in (0.10, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01)]

local_points = vcat(
    [(; label = "m=$(r.m)", r.aware_days, r.final) for r in trigger_sweep],
    [(; label = "α=$(r.α)", r.aware_days, r.final)
     for r in strength_sweep if r.α != 0.5],
)
national_points = [(; label = "θ=$(r.θ)", r.aware_days, r.final)
                   for r in national_sweep]

fig = Figure(size = (880, 440))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "aware person-days taken",
          ylabel = "final epidemic size",
          title = "What each rule achieves for the precaution taken")
for (points, colour, marker, name) in
        ((local_points, :firebrick, :circle, "local information"),
         (national_points, :steelblue, :diamond, "national information"))
    scatter!(ax, [p.aware_days for p in points], [p.final for p in points];
             color = colour, marker = marker, markersize = 13, label = name)
    text!(ax, [p.aware_days for p in points], [p.final for p in points];
          text = [p.label for p in points], color = colour, fontsize = 11,
          offset = (8, 4))
end
hlines!(ax, [baseline.final]; color = :grey, linestyle = :dash)
text!(ax, 12000, baseline.final + 15; text = "nobody reacts", color = :grey,
      fontsize = 12)
xlims!(ax, -1500, 33000)
axislegend(ax; position = :rc)
fig
```

### C1. Interpret

- Both rules apply identical precautions, and in the matched pair about the same
  number of people spend about the same time taking them. Explain, in terms of
  *who* is protected, why the local rule ends with a much smaller epidemic.
- A compartmental SIR model can be given a transmission rate that falls as
  prevalence rises, which is the national rule. Say what it would take to write
  the local rule as a system of differential equations in $S$, $I$ and $R$, and
  why that is the point of this session.
- The local rule assumes people know, at once and for free, how many infectious
  people are within three cells of them. Name two ways that assumption fails in a
  real outbreak, and say for each one whether it would make the local rule look
  better or worse than it does here.
- The national rule at $\theta = 0.01$ does reduce the epidemic substantially.
  Using the figure, say what it is asking of the population to get there and
  whether you would call it a success.
